headline: Bengals’ winding path offers Commanders a road map back to prominence
author: Tashan Reed

paragraphs.text: The Cincinnati Bengals nearly pulled it off. After the 2021 season, they made an improbable run to the Super Bowl before ultimately falling four points shy of upsetting the Los Angeles Rams. It was only quarterback Joe Burrow’s sophomore NFL season, which fed plenty of optimism about what they could accomplish before his big second contract hit the books.

That hope wasn’t shaken when they fell to the eventual Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs in the playoffs a year later. Cincinnati was viewed as a perennial contender that had plenty of financial flexibility to maximize its window.
The Bengals haven’t made the postseason since.

It wasn’t until this year that Cincinnati (7-2) would be regarded as a serious challenger again. The Washington Commanders (3-5-1) want to keep turning their season around when the teams meet Monday night at Northwest Stadium. The Commanders are rightfully focused on the present, not the big picture. That said, their opponent could provide some valuable long-term lessons.
When assessing the Burrow-era Bengals’ winding path back to prominence, a road map emerges for the Jayden Daniels-era Commanders to do the same.

The adversity hit right away for Cincinnati. After getting drafted first overall in 2020, Burrow suffered a torn ACL and MCL in his left knee. While there weren’t questions about his health by the time he signed an extension in September 2023, that wouldn’t last long.

Burrow suffered a season-ending wrist injury later that season. Although he was healthy in 2024, he missed nine games because of turf toe last season. Amid his inability to stay on the field, his cap hit ballooned from about $19.5 million in 2023 to $29.5 million in 2024 and $45.9 million in 2025.

That led to some difficult decisions for Duke Tobin, the Bengals’ director of player personnel. Burrow’s increasingly expensive contract — along with new deals for wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins — led them to lose several core players from their Super Bowl run.
That increased the pressure on Tobin to build the team through the draft. He proved to be capable — of their 22 starters, 14 were drafted or signed by Cincinnati as undrafted free agents.

With that base of homegrown talent, Tobin was freed up to take some risks. He signed left tackle Orlando Brown Jr., defensive end Boye Mafe, defensive tackle Jonathan Allen and safety Bryan Cook to significant free agent contracts in recent years and made a splashy trade for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence this past offseason.

Throughout the roster reconstruction, the Bengals remained committed to head coach Zac Taylor. There were plenty of questions about his job security last winter after they missed the playoffs for the third consecutive season.

Cincinnati made coordinator changes, but they stuck with Taylor. As the franchise reshaped itself around Burrow, the Bengals maintained continuity in the front office and coaching staff. They were criticized at times, but the patience paid dividends.

“With Joe being out, that was obviously a big piece of it for them — he’s such an incredible player,” Commanders Coach Dan Quinn said. “But I think, starting with him, there’s a lot of resiliency and toughness that come throughout the entire team.”

Washington got off to a much faster start with its magical run to the NFC championship game during the 2024 season, when Daniels was a rookie, but they’ve since plummeted. Daniels — and many others throughout the roster — suffered major injuries and doomed a 2025 season that ended with a 5-12 record.

This season also presented challenges. Although Daniels missed just two games after re-dislocating his left elbow in Week 2, several key teammates — Laremy Tunsil, Terry McLaurin, Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw — have gone down with injuries. The Commanders remain alive in the playoff hunt, but their chances of advancing (if they manage to get there) are low.

Changing that will probably require another offseason retooling. The question is whether the tandem of General Manager Adam Peters and Quinn will be handling that. Owner Josh Harris hasn’t made any public decisions, but it’s worth looking ahead, anyway.

To mirror what Cincinnati has pulled off, the Commanders must draft better. Quinn’s game management issues and failure to consistently close out contests have drawn criticism this season, but the roster is flawed. They simply don’t have enough young, ascending talent.

Peters has hit on picks such as Daniels, linebacker Sonny Styles and wide receiver Antonio Williams, but the overall results have been underwhelming. Only six of Washington’s 22 starters were drafted by Peters. The roster also lacks quality depth.
The Commanders have leaned heavily on veteran acquisitions throughout Peters’ tenure. That’s not a recipe for continuous growth.

In the short term, it’s largely on Quinn and Daniels to ensure this regime gets another crack at improving in the offseason. Harris didn’t give Quinn a win total he needs to hit, but he wants to see progress. Given the state of the roster, Daniels will have to play at an elite level for that to happen.

“You don’t really know what you’ve learned until you get into the next season and the next opportunity,” Quinn said. “So, for us, having him playing now and getting back into that over an extended time, that’s winning football.”
It remains to be seen whether that’ll translate to results. Knocking off the Bengals would make their hopes of gaining ground in the NFC East a lot more realistic.
“The proof is in, ‘Can you do it again? Can you do again?’” Quinn said. “That’s what I’m looking for.”
